transcription: If you've ever thought the rules around firearms in America couldn't get any more controversial, the latest Supreme Court 6-3 emergency decision might change everything you think you know about suppressors and short-barreled rifles. Because what just happened inside the nation's highest court isn't just another legal ruling buried in paperwork that nobody reads. It's a decision that could directly impact gun owners, law enforcement practices, federal regulations, and the future definition of what the government can and cannot restrict when it comes to firearm accessories and classifications. And the most shocking part is not just the decision itself, but the reasoning behind it and how quickly it could reshape enforcement across the entire country. To understand why this ruling matters so much, you have to first understand what suppressors and short-barreled rifles actually represent in the legal system. A suppressor, often incorrectly called a silencer, is not a device that makes a gun completely silent like in movies. Instead, it reduces noise and muzzle flash, making shooting safer for hearing protection and more controlled in certain environments. Short-barreled rifles, on the other hand, are rifles with barrels shorter than the standard legal length defined under federal law, and they are heavily regulated under the National Firearms Act. For decades, these two categories have sat at the center of a legal and political debate involving public safety concerns, constitutional rights under the Second Amendment, and the extent of federal regulatory power. The emergency nature of this Supreme Court decision is what immediately raised eyebrows across legal circles. Emergency rulings are not the typical slow, months-long deliberations people expect from the court. Instead, they are fast, high-impact interventions that can temporarily or partially change how laws are applied while larger cases are still being reviewed. A 6-3 split in such a context signals a deeply divided court, where the majority believed immediate action was necessary to address what they saw as an urgent constitutional or procedural issue, while the dissenting justices likely viewed the move as premature or overly disruptive to existing legal frameworks. At the heart of this case is a long-standing challenge to federal restrictions on suppressors and short-barreled rifles. For years, gun rights advocates have argued that these items are not fundamentally different from other regulated firearms accessories, and that requiring extensive registration, taxation, and approval under federal law places an unfair burden on lawful gun owners. On the other side, government attorneys and gun control advocates have maintained that these regulations are essential for tracing ownership, preventing misuse, and maintaining oversight of potentially dangerous modifications to firearms. Number one is the silence from death row. While viewers saw Parker in social media clips, home videos, and police bodycam footage, she was never actually interviewed from prison. Director Jessica Dimmock told USA Today that this was a deliberate creative choice. Rather than centering the narrative on the killer or granting her a platform, the production team chose to exclusively focus on the victims and the families whose lives were permanently shattered by this tragedy. Number two, her mother knew the truth. Parker's mother, Shonda Pryor, also never appeared in the film, yet her courtroom testimony was some of the trial's most explosive. Pryor revealed that she was actually present when Parker underwent a hysterectomy years prior, making a pregnancy physically impossible. title: Change will come, so appreciate the moment | Journal Reading 013
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Today was a good day to haul sugar beets. The sun was shining, the roads were mostly clear, and everyone was in a good mood, laughing and talking, making the best out of 12 hours in a truck. But then it happened. My coworker had a patch of ice just right and jackknifed into the ditch. The truck looked like someone snapped its neck clean around. It wasn't terrible. No one lost their life, but it didn't look good. I've never jackknifed and I hope that I never do. Seeing the truck twisted in an unnatural way gave me pause. It reminded me just how quickly things can change, for better or worse. In this case, worse. I couldn't help but place myself in the driver's seat of that situation. What was it like to dive nose first into the ditch and, at the last second, be snapped in the opposite direction? Had the truck begun to tip before it righted itself? Sometimes things change so quickly we can't keep our wits about us. And other times the change is so slow we drive ourselves insane trying to see results. But either way, whether you want it or not, change will come. For change is the only constant. So before the change comes, take a moment to appreciate where you are, who you are. Because this moment, you'll never get back.

title: SF Game Developers Conference welcomes attendees from 100+ countries | KTVU
transcription:
Daniel, Game Developers Conference started today in San Francisco. Tens of thousands of attendees from big game companies to small independent developers are gathering this week for workshops, game demos, panel discussions on the future of gaming platforms, AI, and other big issues. KTVU's Jana Katsuyama gives us a look at the buzz inside this year's GDC.

The 2024 GDC, Game Developers Conference, kicked off Monday, bringing participants from more than 100 countries to San Francisco's Moscone Center. This year, organizers say they've expanded the scope.

It's not just game developers you'll see this year, as you've seen in the past, but it's everything that goes into making a game and publishing the game and marketing the game. So, you'll see the entire ecosystem of games, including investors, publishers, developers, audio...

Also new this year, a Luminary series for executives to network with industry leaders, and a new Game Commons area with podcasting and a Game Jam where attendees make brand-new games right at the conference. The last GDC drew more than 30,000 people. This year, there are some 1,100 speakers and companies from Xbox and Meta to Roblox, Discord, and smaller independent developers.

Now when I come here, I can connect with all my West Coast friends, friends at studios, and talk about how the industry has changed and connecting with different players. Things that worked, things that haven't. So, it's really great.

See a lot of our users out here. So, every year we can get a lot of really great feedback about what, where are the tooling in the ecosystem lacking.

My biggest thing that I want to get, more people that I network with, more people in the same industry.

AI, of course, is one big factor in many sessions.

There's a lot of discussion around both generative AI as well as agentic AI, working with agents as part of game development pipeline.

Some say they're glad to see more women in the industry and hope that will grow.

The ratio is about 1:25 or 30 maybe, so, so, I think there is, we need to be doing more.

And many people say it's important this year to be face-to-face and network with others at this very critical time for the gaming industry.

Different funding organizations have started to pull their funding from really big, key studios. And what ends up happening is is those studios have to make really hard cuts. And it kind of runs the gamut. It's everything from small studios to even really large, existing studios.

The conference is giving San Francisco's economy a welcome boost. Again, this conference goes all the way to Friday when the last sessions wrap up. Reporting from the Moscone Center in San Francisco, Jana Katsuyama, KTVU, Fox 2 News.

title: Q1 2026 - Quarter In Review | XML Financial Group | Market Commentary
transcription: Welcome. I hope that you had a wonderful Easter or Passover. It was an eventful first quarter of the year. Let's reflect on a few of the major themes. Gas prices were up nearly a dollar a gallon in the first quarter, and when multiplied across millions of households filling up week after week, the cumulative impact on consumer spending and savings rates is significant. However, it's the indirect costs that are possibly more meaningful. Gasoline and diesel fuel are basic inputs to nearly everything the economy produces. Transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, and distribution all depend on energy, which means that higher fuel costs raise the price of goods and services across the board. The stock market saw its share of volatility as well. In Q1, the S&P 500, in blue, we see here was down about 4.3% for the quarter, with the sectors on the left in green being the out-performers, and on the right in red, being the under-performers. The standout on the left is energy, having a terrific start to the year, for perhaps not so terrific reasons. And then many of the sectors that outperformed in the past, on the right, financials, consumer discretionary, technology, not performing especially well, with this highlighting the potential benefits of diversification. So, how does this negative 4.3% return compared to past quarters? Well, this chart shows quarterly S&P 500 returns, ranked from worst on the left to best on the right, going back to 1988. And interestingly, what we see is that the Q1 return from '16 is exactly the same as the Q1 return from '15, -4.3%. Now, interestingly, the other three quarters of '15 happened to be very strong, with Q2 returning 10.9%, Q3, 5.9%, and Q4, 2.7%. This, of course, isn't to suggest that the rest of '16 will be just as the rest of '15 was, but it's a good reminder that often when market participants are most concerned is when the market performs best. Thanks for watching. Enjoy today.

Well, with what we know, in other words, review of all the surveillance information we have with actually getting to hear from one of the- one of the witnesses, one of his best friends that was there throughout the situation, listening to the calls that were made, the Coast Guard contact, as well as the rip tide situation in that area. title: Barron Trump’s emergency call to police
transcription: Just days before his father's second inauguration last January, President Trump's teenage son Barron placed an urgent call for help to police in London. Quote, "I'm calling from the US," Barron Trump told an operator at the UK's 999 emergency line. "I just got a call from a girl, you know, she's getting beat up," adding, "it's really an emergency." That call's transcript, released by prosecutors, now key evidence in the London trial of 22-year-old Russian national, Matvey Rumyantsev, accused of rape and assault, which he denies. The January attack allegedly witnessed in part by Trump, whose late-night video call to the victim was briefly answered by the defendant, whom Trump would describe in an email to prosecutors as a quote "shirtless man with darkish hair," according to British media covering the trial. The victim reportedly praising Trump in testimony Wednesday, quote, "He helped save my life. That call was like a sign from God at that moment." Barron Trump, the only son of the President and First Lady Melania Trump, keeps a low public profile, with no public speeches and few appearances. His father crediting the teen for his help finding ways to reach young voters. "He knew the youth vote..." On the night of the incident, the operator pressed Trump for details about the victim and how he knew her. Quote, "I don't think those details matter. She's getting beat up," Trump replies, adding, "I met her on social media." British media reporting that the defendant testified today that he told the victim in the fall of 2024 that he was quote "upset" about her talking to Barron Trump. Both the White House and the First Lady's office declined to comment on this case. Tom? Garrett, thank you. When we return at six, we thank you for watching, and remember, stay updated on breaking news and top stories on the NBC News app or watch live on our YouTube channel.

title: JonBenét Ramsey's Dad Responds to Claim She's in Epstein Files | E! News
transcription: John Ramsey is setting the record straight about a new rumor involving his daughter JonBenét Ramsey and Jeffrey Epstein. After a TikTok video recently circulated claiming the child beauty queen is in the Epstein files and that the millionaire convicted sex offender had a relationship with her, JonBenét's father is speaking out. Telling TMZ January 27, "Absolutely no truth to it. I haven't seen this but with AI, anything is possible. I figured one of these days I would be accused of being an Epstein pal. Hasn't happened yet. Internet people can be very cruel." The viral video also alleges that Epstein's co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell, who was found guilty on several charges, including sex trafficking of a minor, was at JonBenét's sixth birthday party. Another claim, John denies. E! News has reached out to John for comment, but hasn't yet heard back. These conspiracy theories come 30 years after JonBenét was found sexually assaulted, beaten, and strangled in the basement of her family's Boulder, Colorado home the day after Christmas. Following her death, authorities initially suspected parents John and Patsy Ramsey, however, they were never prosecuted. Patsy later died in 2006, and the case of JonBenét's mysterious murder remains unsolved.

title: Clinics in Dermatology Promo Video
transcription: Hello, I'm Sarah Dyson, a dermatology registrar based in the UK. I'd like to give you a brief introduction to our review for the upcoming special issue in Clinics in Dermatology on GLP-1 receptor agonists. The story of how they were discovered begins in an unexpected place, with a venomous desert lizard called the Gila monster, native to southwestern USA and northwestern Mexico. The Gila monster has remarkable metabolic efficiency, surviving on just a few meals each year. And it was this unusual biology which first attracted scientific interest. As shown on this timeline, research into Gila monster venom led to the discovery of exendin-4 in 1992 by the American endocrinologist John Eng. This was a major breakthrough because exendin-4 shares many of the properties of human GLP-1, but remains active in the body for much longer. Just over a decade later, exenatide became the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, later paving the way for newer drugs such as liraglutide and semaglutide, which have transformed the management of obesity and diabetes. So, why does this matter to dermatologists? Obesity can have a major impact on skin health and is associated with conditions such as psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa, poor wound healing, and increased risk of infection. While GLP-1 receptor agonists are best known for weight loss and improving metabolic health, they may be doing more than that. Emerging evidence suggests that they may have anti-inflammatory effects and influence immune pathways involved in skin disease, with studies showing potential benefits in inflammatory dermatoses, such as psoriasis and hidradenitis suppurativa. In our review, we explore the fascinating history of GLP-1 receptor agonists, from the discovery of exendin-4 in Gila monster venom through to their emerging relevance in dermatology today. Keep an eye out for the special issue, which will be published in Clinics in Dermatology later this year, and we hope you enjoy reading it. Thank you.

title: Spoken-Word Quiet Kind Of Heavy
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
Lingering memories follow him
like shadows along the wall
The echoes of a screaming past
refusing to fall
Chaos
crashing through his chest
lightning strikes in his lungs, thunder roars in his thoughts and
grey skies left standing there alone and
torn
untamed storm
His mind on endless repeat
every ache silent, looping, every wound carved deeper
heavier
every piece of his soul it chose to take
moment by moment, it consumes a little more
torment after torment
and in the quiet
he whispers
am I something I can't restore?
He begins to feel unfamiliar
a stranger in his own skin
where safety is a memory and fear is moving near
filling every corner of his own mind, every breath, every thought, every space
until even peace feels like
a forgotten place
And still, he searches for calm in the night
finding refuge in fractured light
from the demons that dance
just beyond his sight
His healing moves slow
but it moves
through roads that twist
through paths that bruise
a journey that tests the strength of his soul
yet step by step
he regains control
head held high, eyes sharp awake
though exhaustion whispers
he's still there
because something inside him refuses to break
refuses to bend, refuses to fade
He won't
he can't
a silent vow
through the dark he'll devour
to reclaim his light
from his own shadowed hour

title: Sustainability Strategy Masterclass: Industry Best Practices
transcription: Reinventing the wheel doesn't add value or drive change, whether that's to sustainability strategy or to a carbon footprint. So I always recommend taking a bit of time before you begin designing your sustainability strategy to look at what else is out there. Um, most organizations can benefit from looking at the UN sustainable development goals and the greenhouse gas protocol, and this will give you ideas of potential topics for your pillars, for your focus areas. It's also really important to look at what regulation that your organization either needs to comply with today or is likely to have to comply with tomorrow, because what you don't want is a central sustainability strategy and then an add-on, "this is how we will comply with EUDR", for example. You want a single sustainability strategy that shows, "these are what's important to us, this is how we're going to move the needle, oh, and whilst we do this, this is how we're going to comply with all of the regulation". And then equally, it's always a good idea to look at what your competitors are doing, um, because if you're working in the same industry, you're likely to be facing the same challenges and whilst each organization is unique and I would never expect two sustainability strategies to be the same, it can just be a really good starting point to help you start thinking thematically about where you want to be looking. So, just on that note, these are the sustainable development goals and these are really broad themes that, I, I find it a really useful exercise with any organization to sit down with the sustainability manager or the health and safety and environment manager or the finance officer, whoever it is who's been tasked with coming up with the sustainability strategy and going through these SDGs and saying, "which really apply to your business, how is your business contributing towards climate action, quality education?" and normally two or three will come out that are incredibly relevant to the business and that can be kind of used as the foundation for how that business should think about sustainability.

title: How to Bullet Journal in 2026 (Every New Technique)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: There's a quiet rebellion happening against the algorithm life, a return to the physical world. Australia just passed a law against young people accessing social media, no-phone cafes are popping up in big cities around the world, and traditional gyms are slowly losing ground to wellness centers focused on health and community. These all address a need that can only be met in the physical world: connection. Nowhere is this need for connection more necessary than with yourself. What are you thinking, feeling, doing about your life? Hi, I'm Ryder Carroll, the creator of the Bullet Journal Method, and today, I want to show you why a paper notebook just might be the most radical productivity tool you can use this year. I'll also include specific ways that the Bullet Journal Method has evolved to help us navigate an increasingly busy, digital, and disconnected world. Let's dive in. Bullet Journal is not a notebook or a type of paper. It's a personal operating system that helps you write a better life. We use notebooks as our preferred platform to run that operating system because it helps us go offline and think with less distractions. That said, you can Bullet Journal in any app you would like. So how does this operating system actually work? Here are the four main steps. Record: This is about creating a record of your life using one-sentence journal entries to capture your notes, actions, moods, and events. Each is paired with a symbol to visually categorize them, hence, Bullet Journal. Reflect: This is about regularly reading your record. As the saying goes, "You don't learn from experience, you learn by reflecting on experience." We do this through practicing daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly reflection rituals. These help us become more aware of patterns in our thinking, feeling, and doing that are impacting our lives. Refine: This is about applying any insights we gain from reflection. It's about cutting what isn't working and cultivating what is, which brings us to the last step. Respond: Respond is the most critical step. It's the step that takes us out of our notebooks into the world by taking intentional action based on all the previous steps.

title: I Found My Old Journal...I Didn't Recognize Myself.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I found an old journal recently. I don't date my entries, I've never been good at that, but I can tell when it was because of the entries around it. But, I can tell that this one is an older one, it's from before my mother passed away. This is hard. I don't know how to be seen. I keep thinking I will open up my mouth and something will come out that makes sense of me, but it never does. I look at other people and it seems so easy for them. They just exist and people respond to them like they matter. I feel like I'm always just on the edge of everything. I want to be heard. I want to express myself. I want to be someone who has something inside of them that's worth noticing. But I don't think there is. Sometimes I think it would just be easier if I just wasn't here. Just... if I disappeared, I wouldn't have to keep failing as a person. This was before my mother died.

title: "5 Journal Prompts For When You Have Nothing To Write"
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: you one more thing. That journal has really helped me a lot to cope up with lots of things. My anxiety, my overthinking, and a lot. So, now moving towards our prompt three, which is, "What is something I keep putting off and why?" Now, this one is a little uncomfortable, and that's exactly why it works. Your journal is the one place where you can be completely honest with yourself. When you write down what you are avoiding and the real reason behind it, it suddenly feels a lot less scary. Sometimes, just naming it is enough to finally do something about it. Now prompt four, "If today were a color, what would it be? And why?" This one sounds simple, but it makes you think creatively about your emotions. Maybe today felt grey and heavy, maybe it felt like a warm yellow. There's no wrong answer, it's just a gentle way to check in with yourself without overthinking it. You would be surprised how much this one reveals and how helpful it is. Now, moving towards our prompt five, which is, what do I need to hear, I mean, "What do I need to hear today that nobody is telling me? What is something that I need to know about me?" So, this is my personal favorite, and all you can do is write it like a letter to yourself. Tell yourself what you actually need, whether that's encouragement, permission to rest, or even a reminder that you are doing better than you think. Be your own person who shows up for you on the hard days. And you don't need to use all five in one sitting. Pick just one, set a timer for 5 minutes, and just write. Some days, your journal will be two lines, some days, it will be three pages, both are perfect. And I'm sure this must have been helpful. I'll see you in the next one. Till then, take care and keep writing.

title: I Found My Grandfather's Old Journal, and What I Read Shocked Me!
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We live our days as if we have an endless supply of tomorrows. But every spring here in Japan, the cherry blossoms remind us of a truth we often try to ignore. A beautiful life isn't one that lasts forever. It is one that blooms fully before the wind takes it away. Every spring, the entire country stops to watch the sakura open. People gather under the trees, lay out blankets, and share food, tea, and be happy together. It's a tradition called Hanami. But if you've never experienced this exact thing in your life, you might not realize what makes the sakura so deeply connected to how we experience life. They only bloom for about 10 to 14 days, sometimes even less. A single strong wind or an early heavy rain can take them all away in one night. And that is exactly why they are so beautiful. If cherry blossoms stayed on the trees forever, nobody would stop to look at them. Since everyone sitting under those trees knows that this moment will not last, they pay attention. They just sit there and soak it in, feeling a deep stillness, aware that the petals are already falling. When I was younger, I used to live as if time was unlimited. I would waste entire days doing things I didn't care about. I would stay in situations that made me unhappy, telling myself I'd change things later. I felt this constant pressure to do everything faster and achieve more, while consistently postponing the things I truly wanted to do. This truth about time really hit me when my grandfather, Daiki, passed away. It happened so quickly that one season, he was sitting with me in his garden, pouring tea and telling me stories. And the next season, his chair was empty, like a petal falling from a branch. After he passed, I was going through his things and found an old journal entry he had written during his last spring. I carry his words with me every single day. He wrote, "Hiroto, the real tragedy of life is how many of our years we waste. The sakura never worries about tomorrow's wind."

Reflecting on these deeper insights helps you make decisions that are in alignment with your true desires rather than simply reacting to external pressures. It's a therapeutic process that helps you gain clarity, reduce confusion, and trust yourself more deeply. Reflective journaling encourages you to get quiet, listen, and tap into the answers already within you. This practice can help you make clearer decisions, find your true path, and reduce inner conflict. By strengthening your connection to your intuition, you can feel more confident in your choices and direction in life. Incorporating reflective journaling into your daily routine provides a powerful way to regain mental clarity and emotional balance. It gives you the space to process your thoughts, align with your core values, and move forward with confidence and purpose. There you have it. These five journaling practices can feel just like therapy, helping you process emotions, gain clarity, and boost your mental well-being. Whether you're writing down your thoughts, challenging negative beliefs, expressing gratitude, or listening to your inner voice, journaling offers a safe and powerful outlet for self-reflection and growth. If you're looking for a way to improve your mental health, reduce stress, and gain a deeper understanding of yourself, these journaling practices are a great place to start. Make journaling a part of your daily routine and watch how it transforms your mindset and emotional state over time. transcription: counter-intuitively, just how well it's been doing recently. Um, it's had gone on a roaring bull run over the past year. At the start of this year, traders talk about prices going parabolic, you know, just shooting up and seeming to go towards the moon. What can happen after that, though, is very large swings in prices, and we actually saw that a few weeks ago. The gold price dropped by about 9% in a single day and then swung wildly afterwards. When you see an asset that is supposed to be a hedge behaving like that, you might feel a little less confident that it's actually going to be a hedge. If it can swing so wildly, is it really a safe haven? And are there any other alternatives, then? Again, counter-intuitively, perhaps the best way to hedge stock market risk is with other stocks. So, I looked at a study that analysts at Goldman Sachs did recently on hedges that would have performed particularly well during the dot-com bubble. And, intriguingly, they found that some of the best ones were select baskets of stocks. So, for example, stocks that pay very high, reliable dividends. So, they offer you a reliable income. They did well on the way up and the way down during the dot-com crash. Stocks with low volatility, this kind of dependable old companies. It might feel a little unsatisfying to say the best way to hedge your stock market risk is with other stocks. But, when you look at the alternatives and how these have performed in the past, it might be the best that investors can do. So, it does sound like there's no way to bubble proof your strategy. Maybe no way to completely bubble proof it, but there is a boring answer here, which is that the one safest investment strategy is buy and hold for the long term. Investors that rode out the dot-com bubble on the way up and on the way down and then held on for the following years, they still ended up doing very well. The very worst thing you can do is sell your stocks during the depths of a crash when you actually lose your money. It's about helping people live fuller, healthier lives. And increasingly, researchers are listening. So, if you're listening and wondering, why should I care about a healthcare conference happening in London? Here's why. Because these meetings help shape the future of care. They influence what our doctors learn, what treatments move forward, what researchers prioritize, and how patient experiences are incorporated into medicine. And while patients may not be physically in every room, organizations like GHLF work hard to make sure patient voices are represented. At its best, medicine is collaborative. Researchers, clinicians, patient advocates, and patients themselves all bring different perspectives, and conferences like EULAR create a space where those perspectives can come together. That does not mean every exciting study becomes a breakthrough overnight, but it does mean progress happens faster when people share ideas, challenge assumptions, and keep patients at the center of the conversation. transcription: Fourth, Management Fee. This entry may look similar to Fund Expense, but the business meaning is different. Assume 2 million management fee is accrued. Debit Management Fee Expense, 2 million. Credit Management Fee Payable, 2 million. At accrual, NAV reduces. If paid later, debit Management Fee Payable, credit Cash. Payment settles the liability. It does not create the expense again. Senior line: accrual moves NAV, payment settles cash. Fund expense is usually paid to a vendor. Management fee is paid to the GP or investment manager. Same looking entry, different PE economics. Fifth, Fair Value Gain. This is a major PE fund accounting trap. Cost was 15 million. Fair value is 18 million. Unrealized gain is 3 million. Debit Investment, 3 million. Credit Unrealized Gain, 3 million. Cash does not move, but NAV increases because fair value moved. LP reporting shows unrealized appreciation. The trap: NAV can increase without cash coming in. This is paper gain until exit. Sixth, Exit or Realization. The fund exits at 18 million. Debit Cash, 18 million. Credit Investment, 18 million. Cash comes in, investment is removed. But if you stop here, your answer is incomplete. The 3 million gain was earlier unrealized. After sale, it becomes realized. Missing entry: debit Unrealized Gain, 3 million. Credit Realized Gain, 3 million. This does not create new profit, it changes the classification of profit. Exit proceeds are 18 million. Cost was 15 million. Realized gain is 3 million. They are not the same number. Seventh, Distribution to LPs. The fund distributes 5 million. Debit Investor Capital, 5 million

title: Journal Your Best Reality ✨ How to Manifest Your Dream Life Through Writing.

transcription: the magic happens. I also want to mention something that people often skip, and that is addressing the resistance. Sometimes while I am writing, a little voice in my head says that is never going to happen. Instead of ignoring that voice, I write it down. I acknowledge the fear and then I consciously pivot. I will write, "I understand why I feel nervous, but I am choosing to believe in my potential." Dealing with these mental blocks on paper takes away their power. You are not just ignoring the obstacles, you are moving through them. This makes your journaling practice feel authentic and honest rather than forced. Another technique I love is the 369 method. You write your intention three times in the morning, six times in the afternoon, and nine times at night. It sounds repetitive because it is, and that repetition is what drills the intention into your subconscious. It keeps your desire at the forefront of your mind all day long. When you are constantly thinking about your goal, you start to notice opportunities that you might have missed before. You start taking inspired action because you are finally aligned with what you want. The most important part of this whole process is letting go after you are done writing. You cannot be desperate for the outcome. Think of it like ordering food at a restaurant. Once you place the order, you do not go into the kitchen to check on the chef every two minutes. You trust that it is being prepared, and it is on its way. Journaling is your way of placing the order. Once you close that book, go live your life, be present, be happy, trust that the reality you have described is already manifesting in the background. Consistency is what makes this truly transformative. It is better to journal for 5 minutes every single day than for 2 hours once a month. Make it a ritual that you actually look forward to. Light a candle, put on some calming music, and give yourself this time to dream without limits. You deserve to live a life that feels as good on the inside as it looks on the outside. I really hope this inspires you to pick up a pen and start designing your best reality today. Your words have so much power, and your future self is waiting for you to claim what is yours. If you found this helpful, I would love for you to subscribe and join our community of creators. Let me know in the comments one thing you are manifesting right now because writing it down publicly is a huge first step to making it real. Thanks so much for watching and I will see you in the next one.

category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The first time I noticed this was on a holiday where I felt a mix of disappointment, nervousness, and was grumpy at the same time for no major reason. Number five, frequent colds and illness. Gym sessions left me wrecked, then bam, sore throat, flu. Overtraining weakens immunity. I got sick like clockwork every two to three months or when I felt I overdid it in the gym or run. Number six, dropping performance, more effort, worse results. Slower times, lower VO2 Max, more effort on the weights. Your gains reverse when your nervous system is fried. It is frustrating but you think, okay, I am just plateauing, it is what it is. Now, if you spot any of these, you might be on the edge of a nervous system overload. But don't worry, this is fixable. We will look at the solutions to this. But first, why is this happening? Let's deep dive so you understand the underlying mechanism within your body. And I really encourage you to look up the podcasts of Andrew Huberman, who can explain it more eloquently than I can. It was an eye-opener to me. At the heart is the HPA axis, your body's built-in alarm system. HPA stands for hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal. Think of it as a relay team. Your brain's hypothalamus spots stress, like intense workouts. Signals the pituitary gland to release a hormone called ACTH, which tells your adrenal glands, on top of your kidneys, to pump out cortisol, the stress hormone. Normally, this is awesome. It gives you quick energy bursts, sharpens focus, and calms inflammation so you can handle life's curveballs. But in overtraining, it's like hitting the alarm non-stop, overloading your system and your body thinking it is in stress all the time. Result, elevated heart rate, tense muscles, sleep disruption. But here's the escape hatch. The cat, hockey stick, ego approach. Number one, be a cat. Prioritise sleep. Ditch the 6:00 a.m. grind if you're clocking under seven hours sleep. It's a burnout trap. Prioritise seven to eight hours of killer sleep, targeting 1.5 to 2 hours of REM and 1 to 1.5 hours deep sleep for peak recovery.

title: Anxiety Treatment
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Dobar dan. Ja sam Ivana Matović sa klinike Med Tim. Danas govorimo o anksioznosti, jednoj od najčešćih stanja sa kojima se savremeni čovjek suočava, a koja se nažalost često predugo trpi pre nego što se prizna. Da odmah razjasnimo, anksioznost nije obična trema. Nije zabrinutost pred važan događaj i nije nešto što treba ignorisati kada počne da traje i počne da vam remeti svakodnevni život. Anksioznost je stanje stalne unutrašnje napetosti, straha i iščekivanja da će se nešto loše dogoditi. Ono što je u njoj najteže, za razliku od običnog straha koji ima jasan povod, anksioznost često nema. Osoba osjeća nemir i strepnju, čak i onda kada objektivno nema nikakve opasnosti. Tu treba biti pošten. Anksioznost u nekim trenucima nije neprijatelj. Kada se nađemo pred izazovom ili neizvjesnošću, tijelo se aktivira da nas pripremi. To je onaj poznati mehanizam: bori se ili bježi. Srce ubrza, disanje se ubrza, mišići se zategnu, pažnja se izoštri. To je korisno, ali na kratko. Problem počinje kada se stanje intenzivira. Tada anksioznost prestaje da bude odbrana, postaje teret koji iscrpljuje. Kako se anksioznost osjeća? Ona se prvo javi u tijelu: ubrzan rad srca, pritisak u grudima, kratak dah ili osjećaj knedle u grlu, vrtoglavica, znojenje, drhtanje, napetost u mišićima. Niz tegoba zbog kojih čovjek prvo pomisli da je nešto ozbiljno sa srcem ili sa zdravljem. Onda odete kod ljekara i nalazi su uredni, jer uzrok najčešće nije u tijelu. Uzrok je u pojačanoj napetosti nervnog sistema. Uporedo ide i ono u glavi: stalna zabrinutost, pretjerano razmišljanje, osjećaj da gubite kontrolu nad sopstvenim mislima, nesanica, razdražljivost, nemir koji ne prestaje. A kod izraženih oblika javlja se i panični napad. Nagli talas straha, praćen lupanjem srca, gušenjem, osjećajem da će se nešto strašno dogoditi. I zato je važno čuti ovo: panični napad jeste zastrašujući, ali sam po sebi najčešće nije opasan po život. To je reakcija organizma na napetost, a ne znak da vam se tijelo gasi. Kada anksioznost traži liječenje? Kada traje, kada je prejaka, kada počnete da izbegavate ljude, posao, obaveze, mesta, kada vam strah krade san i koncentraciju i posebno kada se panični napadi i stalna napetost jave bez jasnog razloga. Jer anksioznost koja traje mjesecima rijetko prolazi sama.

title: Staying | The Cost of Choosing Loyalty Over Safety
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The hardest battles are often fought in silence. Behind polite smiles, behind tired eyes, behind voices that still say, "I'm fine." Some people carry storms so quietly that even the people closest to them never fully see the rain. And sometimes, the mind becomes heavy for so long that exhaustion starts feeling normal. Thoughts repeat themselves, doubts grow louder. The world slowly loses color and people begin believing they are far less important than they truly are. Pain has a way of shrinking perspective. It whispers things that sound permanent during temporary seasons. It tells tired hearts that nothing will change, that peace belongs to other people, that healing was never meant for them. And slowly, the weight of those thoughts begins to feel real. But thoughts are not always truth. Some people are not trying to leave life behind, they are simply trying to escape the heaviness of carrying everything alone. The pressure, the expectations, the loneliness hidden beneath functioning lives. And sometimes, the people who seem strongest are simply the ones who learned how to suffer quietly. Not because they are weak, but because they became used to surviving silently. One day at a time, sometimes one hour at a time, and occasionally, one breath at a time, there is no shame in surviving slowly. None of us truly know how deeply we are woven into the lives of others. Sometimes, we minimize our importance because pain has made us forget how much of our presence...

title: When You're Depressed and Feel Alone: A Message for Your Darkest Days
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
Through it. Not to minimize your pain, to remind you you are in good company, even if it doesn't feel that way. When you're depressed, there are voices. Not literal voices, but thoughts that feel like voices. And they lie. Let me name them for you, because naming things gives us power over them. The voice of isolation: "No one understands. No one cares. You're completely alone." The voice of worthlessness: "You're a burden. Everyone would be better off without you. You have nothing to offer." The voice of hopelessness: "This will never end. You'll feel like this forever. There's no point in trying." The voice of guilt: "You should be grateful. Other people have it worse. What's wrong with you?" The voice of exhaustion: "You're too tired to fight. Just give up. It's easier." But these voices are not you. They are symptoms. Like a cough is a symptom of a cold, they are the depression talking, not your truth. And here's what I need you to understand: you don't have to believe everything you think. But I'm not going to give you a list of 10 easy steps to beat depression, because that would be insulting. But I am going to share some things that help, not cure, help when nothing else helps. 

1. The one-minute rule. When everything feels impossible, give yourself permission to do something for just one minute. One minute of fresh air. One minute of stretching. One minute of writing. One minute of sitting in silence. After one minute, you can stop. But often, one minute becomes two. Two becomes five. And suddenly, you've done something. 

2. The smallest victory. Depression steals your sense of accomplishment. Fight back by counting the smallest victories. You brushed your teeth? Victory. You got out of bed? Victory. You ate something? Victory. You're still here? The biggest victory of all. Write these down. Small victories are still victories. 

3. The compassionate voice. When the voices of depression speak, talk back, but not with anger. With compassion. If a friend was hurting, what would you say to them? Say that to yourself. "I see you're struggling. That's okay. You don't have to be okay right now. This is really hard, and you're still here. That's incredible. I love you, even when you can't love yourself." 

4. The anchor. Find one thing that anchors you to the present moment. Your breath. The feeling of your feet on the floor. A warm cup of tea. A familiar song. A photo that brings a tiny flicker of something. When the darkness threatens to pull you under, reach for your anchor. Hold on, just for now.

title: Inside Robinhood's Original Pitch Deck: Why Investors Said Yes
transcription: In 2013, two Stanford math graduates named Vladimir Tenev and Baiju Bhatt attempted to pitch a radical concept: zero commission stock trading managed entirely through a mobile phone. At this point, they had been entrepreneurs for the better part of five years. They had built several pieces of financial software for high frequency firms, but they had very little tangible success to show for that time. When they tried to raise money for Robinhood, they ran a brutal gauntlet. They were rejected 70 times, then 90 times. Eventually, 110 investors told them no. The feedback was consistent: professional investors didn't believe people would manage their finances on a smartphone. They looked at the founders' math backgrounds and dismissed them as being incapable of building a product for regular consumers. Many founders react to this kind of rejection by treating their pitch deck like a sales brochure. They try to hide their lack of traction behind flashy design elements or unrealistic multi-billion dollar projections. Robinhood took a different path. They realized that before a deck can sell a product, it has to prove the founders are worthy of trusting. Vlad and Baiju began a process of ruthless subtraction. Instead of adding slides to answer every objection, they cut the presentation down to its absolute essentials. They removed the industry jargon and the dense maps of the financial ecosystem. They focused the entire narrative on one universal problem: the high cost and unnecessary friction of the traditional brokerage model. They avoided the trap of pitching a vague, massive market. Instead, their narrative shrinks the opportunity down to a single, sharp data point. They targeted an underserved generation of millennials wanting to invest, but frustrated by $10 commission fees. This narrow focus made it difficult for investors to dismiss the idea with broad generalizations. By proving they understood one user group better than anyone else, they signaled a level of competence that forced investors to take them seriously. But the digital slides are only half the battle. Eventually, that trust has to be validated by the founders in the room. This reached a breaking point during a meeting with Tim Draper...

title: Does Civic AI Mean? | Ron Ivey (Noēsis Collaborative) | Civic AI Conference 2026
transcription: With the question that we've been wrestling with today about how should AI care for communities and who gets to decide, I think one of the challenges I have is the it's kind of very fundamental uh kind of premise of that question, whether AI can care. From what I understand and from, you know, talking to and working with uh the developers of these systems, there's there's a real debate whether AI actually cares, where whether it actually has the capacity for empathy, uh whether it has the capacity for moral consideration of others, attentiveness to others, and and really understanding others' uh feelings and perceptions. We already heard this morning about how, you know, the systems themselves cannot distinguish between these issues of of parental sacrifice, which I'm a parent, I'm having to sacrifice every day in terms of my relationships, and child sacrifice. So, just that fundamental understanding of relationship of relational language uh these systems don't understand. So, can an AI care? I don't think so, but could an AI system be designed to support care, to support human relationships? Well, we had already have some great examples from today's conference uh of both in the context of democracy, the use of of AI as a tool to support uh participation uh and engagement and real understanding and legitimacy of bills that are being passed related to synthetic media. That's exciting. Uh we have the application of AI to support uh care and relationship in the healthcare context, in terms of what's happening related to to some of the patients and and getting data that their caregivers can can improve the care. That's exciting as well. And then, in terms of who gets to decide, I think it goes back to this fundamental question of how these systems are built and the power that's that's driving them. Do we have the right kind of cultural framework, uh ethical framework, and the right kind of policy framework to decentralize uh power and decentralize the way these markets are concentrated right now? Until we do that, until we fundamentally deal with the market concentration, the wealth concentration, the power concentration, we'll have challenges on a broader scale in terms of really implementing AI systems that support both those intimate, close relationships and then as the relationships expand into these larger uh contexts of solidarity and trust. Now, that being said, we do have an opportunity, even in the midst of the dominant systems, to to create an alternative ecosystem. To think about funders and investors and inventors and and researchers and policy uh uh experts and local activists and community uh groups. I, you know, seeing inspiring things at the local level where communities are taking control and building their own models, and that's exciting. So, even if we have a dominant system that's can continue to move forward in one direction, there might be a pathway, and I'm hopeful there is a pathway, for alternative systems. It's just about encouraging those and and supporting them and and finding the right kind of resources and uh connecting the dots between those that are doing incredible things in different communities around the world.

title: Scientists studied doomscrolling. Here’s what they found.
transcription: Tell us what you found about the weakening of our cognitive skills and its relationship with our devices, and particularly with short-form videos. Mhm. There's not a ton of research. There are a few studies, and, and we really want to look for experimental studies, because there's plenty of correlational research, which tells us that people who say they spend a lot of time consuming social media also show that they're having trouble with some cognitive skills. But that could be, you know, a reverse causation, where people who have some trouble with cognitive skills find themselves, um, unable to look away from these feeds. So, I wanted to find experimental studies where you could actually randomize people, do a, a treatment, and then see if there's a difference. And there are a couple of studies that have basically given a cognitive test and then exposed the participants to 10 minutes, 30 minutes of scrolling on either TikTok or Twitter or YouTube. You know, they tried these different forms of media, and then they would redo the test and see if there was a difference in their performance before and after that, you know, scrolling. And there are a couple of studies that have shown that these short-form video feeds specifically are affecting cognitive skills even with that very short exposure. And they're small studies. I would like to see them repeated and expanded. But they do suggest that skills like being able to pause and, and be critical about what you're think, what you're looking at, and skills like remembering to do something that you intended to do, those are the skills that we're seeing impacted by even just a short exposure to something like TikTok. So, what I found super interesting in what you found and in the video that you've done on this is that there's even a difference between scrolling, the physical action of scrolling through TikTok, and if those same TikTok videos of a cat or a dog or whatever it is are merged together in a kind of like a montage style. That, that there's something about the act of literally physically scrolling as opposed to just watching, even if the content is the same content, that affects our brains in different ways. Is that, am I getting it right? Yes, that's exactly right. And that was one of the things that was really surprising to me because I thought it was just, 'Oh, short content is probably harming our attention spans.' But it's not that the content is short. It's that it's this style of interacting where you kind of decide really quickly whether you're going to watch it or not with this swiping interface. If we're forced to just watch a long string of videos, you don't see that deficit in the cognitive performance that you see when you're interacting with these apps as they're designed. And that design is actually key to making them work. And so, it's kind of built in, which led me to wonder whether we should even continue to make this form of content. Do you know why that is, Jess? Did you get a sense of why, of why, what it is about our scrolling as opposed to just watching a montage?

Broke pieces of my body I'm still paying for, surgery waiting, trust gone cold, institutions I'll never look at the same, for some brothers it becomes a revolving door, easier inside than out, simpler, safer in the trap. Distractions everywhere, good ones, loud ones, beautiful ones, and sometimes in the middle of a project, focus slipping, noise rising, I close my eyes and remember the quiet of that cell. Prison took, prison gave, and the parting gift, I'm still learning how to keep. I said it, I miss my prison cell. Not the place, the clarity it forced on me, and I'm trying. God knows I'm trying to find that same quiet here, in the middle of freedom.

title: When You're Depressed and Feel Alone: A Message for Your Darkest Days
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You don't have to see the other side. You just have to build the bridge, one plank at a time. Today's plank: breathe. Tomorrow's plank: text one person. Next week's plank: take one short walk. You're not trying to cross the ocean. You're just building enough to get through today. What no one tells you about healing from depression: it's not linear. You'll have good days. You'll think, "I'm better," and then a bad day will hit you like a wave and you'll feel like you're back at the beginning. This is normal. This is healing. Two steps forward, one step back. Still progress. It's not quick. You didn't get here overnight. You won't leave here overnight. Be patient with yourself. Give yourself the time you need. It's not something you do alone. Asking for help is not weakness. It's the strongest thing you can do. A therapist, a doctor, a trusted friend, a support group. You don't have to carry this alone. And it doesn't mean you'll never hurt again. Healing doesn't mean the pain disappears forever. It means you develop the tools to handle it when it comes. It means the waves get smaller and you get stronger. Can I say something directly to you now? Not to everyone, just to you. I don't know your name. I don't know your story. I don't know what brought you here, but I know this: you are still here, despite everything, despite every voice that told you to give up, despite every day that felt impossible, despite every night that felt endless. You are still here, and that means something. That means you're fighting. Even if it doesn't feel like fighting. Even if it feels like barely surviving. Surviving is fighting. Staying is fighting. Breathing is fighting. And you're doing it right now, in this moment. Depression lies. It tells you you're alone. You're not. It tells you it will never end. It will. It tells you you're broken. You're not broken. You're healing, even if it doesn't feel like it. So here's what I want you to do after this video ends: take one breath. Just one. Then take another. Then do one small thing for yourself. Anything. A glass of water, a blanket, a message to someone who cares. And then tomorrow, do it again. Not because it's easy, because you're worth it. You are worth it. Even when you can't feel it, even when you can't believe it, you are worth it. I'm proud of you for being here. I mean that. Now breathe, and keep going. One moment at a time.

And the reason for this, largely, has been school. Each generation spends more time in school. We use school to develop our cognition. Congratulations, you see your correlation. Until Gen Z. transcription: While Republicans have lost credibility on the economy, that hasn't automatically benefited Democrats. Minnesota needs a comprehensive state economic plan. Agriculture accounts for roughly 15% of the state's total economic output and supports over 320,000 jobs. Tariffs and climate volatility have made farming increasingly precarious, an opportunity for the DFL to build a stability plan. Meanwhile, Minnesota's urban centers are scrambling. Minneapolis pins hope on the 2028 DFL Draft, but one-off events are short-term boosts. Most of that revenue flows to downtown hotels and restaurants, not throughout the regional economy. We need something with real reach. Rochester offers one model, a strategic focus on healthcare and life sciences, advanced manufacturing, technology and software, and education. We don't need to copy it, but we do need a regional plan that actively encourages businesses to locate here. Right now, a company considering Minneapolis faces a wall of regulations and taxes first. Amenities like parks, schools, and community come second, if at all. Outsiders see instability and chaos. They are, there are real differences between the state's DFL's message and Minneapolis's more DSA-aligned wing. But unless you're deeply embedded in local politics, you won't grasp those distinctions. What you see instead is a city divided, one that seems hostile to the conditions that attract jobs and investment. The math is simple, we cannot shrink the tax base by driving out employers while expanding government employment. Immigration. Minneapolis residents earned the recognition they received for their response to ICE enforcement. At great personal risk, many stepped between federal agents and their immigrant neighbors. We showed the world what people-powered resistance looks like when facing government overreach. But what's next? Opposing Trump is part of the answer, though without Senate control, Democrats will be reduced to Instagram complaints. The harder work begins with sanctuaries that actually function. Minneapolis welcomed a large influx of Ecuadorians fleeing gang violence and economic collapse. That was the right call, but it requires a real plan.

title: Lifestyle Journal: The Playbook For Health, Wealth, Strength and Purpose by Miguel Hernandez
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Then, the day transitions into time blocking. Throw out that messy, overwhelming to-do list, and use priority and focus blocks instead. And the evening, it isn't just about crashing on the couch. It's a dedicated closure ritual. Doing a digital sunset and some light journaling helps reset your nervous system and gets your body ready for deep restorative sleep. If you design your day well, your life is just going to naturally follow. Now let's talk about the load-bearing pillars. Section three, health and strength. Hernandez breaks life down into five deeply connected segments. The key here is that health and strength aren't just these separate isolated chores you try to frantically squeeze in on the weekends. They are connected, equal pieces of a unified life system. It's like a structure. If one of these segments is neglected, the whole thing starts to lean and eventually, it could collapse. Let's zoom in on health for a second. For Hernandez, health is your ultimate absolutely non-negotiable asset. It's not just a goal you hit, it is the fundamental baseline of your human potential. So, no fad diets here, just sustainable nourishment using whole foods and balanced macros. He frames movement as your daily medicine, and sleep, sleep is literally your body's essential nightly repair crew. He also gives a pretty stark warning that chronic stress is like a silent structural rot. That's exactly why tools like breathwork and nervous system resets are so incredibly vital in your daily blueprint. And building right on top of health, we have strength. Now, we aren't just talking about how much weight you can lift in the gym. True strength is defined as the ability to remain grounded under pressure. Sure, it encompasses physical longevity, but it's also about having the mental clarity to stay intensely focused. It's having the emotional literacy to consciously respond to whatever life throws at you instead of impulsively reacting to it. It is all about building rock solid inner stability. All right, let's move to section four, wealth, purpose and connection. Think of this as the mortar holding everything together. I absolutely love how Hernandez completely redefines this concept. True wealth is not about impulsive luxury spending or showing off, it's actually about building a repeatable system that grants you ultimate freedom, optionality, and total peace of mind. It's about increasing your value by building skills, spending consciously in a way that aligns with your true values, and playing the long game with investing. It's not magic, it's a learnable system. Alongside wealth, we have purpose and connection. You know, purpose isn't some mystical treasure you just magically stumble upon. It's an emotional engine that you have to actively build right at the intersection of your strengths, and how you can serve others. And you don't do this alone, you build it alongside an aligned community.

title: How to Bullet Journal in 2026 (Every New Technique)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Now, I used to start writing about what I should do, resolutions and goals to achieve certain outcomes. It began every year with all this pressure and burden that never ended up working out all that well. These days, I start my New Year's chapter in a less stressful way by setting clear intentions. I do this by writing them down at the beginning of my notebook. Here's a simple formula to set your intention: Who + What + Why. Be, who, an attribute of the kind of person, what, in what context or area of your life, so that, why, the reason that it matters. For example, be curious with my challenges so that I may learn instead of getting stuck. Be steady in moments of stress so that I may respond rather than react. Be honest with my communication so that my relationships may feel authentic. Be committed to my movement so that I may reduce the suffering of an idle mind. Who + What + Why. My intention is a commitment to a process. Maybe it's the process of being a healthier person, an authentic leader, or a present partner. I base that commitment on what I learned in the previous chapter of my life. Committing to a process rather than an outcome is a much more forgiving approach because it embraces the truth. I've no idea how to be that way yet. It's a story that I'm learning how to live, one moment at a time. It doesn't really take all that much to start writing a better life. All you need is an intention, a notebook, something to write with, and a practice of writing in your notebook in a way that moves that intention forward. If you need help building your bullet journal practice or getting any of your questions answered along the way, learning how to practice Name and Tame, for example, as you write your own story, check out the Foundation Plan. You'll get every resource that you need and live sessions to practice these techniques with people from around the world to move beyond basic productivity to a practice that can help you transform your relationship with your time, your life, and yourself this year. And if you want to hit the ground running and set up your notebook the right way, watch this video next. It'll help you get started without getting stuck or worried that you're not doing it the right way. Thank you for taking the time, and see you in the next one.

title: International Women’s Day 2026 Theme | Rights. Justice. Action. | Give To Gain | UN Women
transcription: gain. Giving is not a loss, giving is multiplication. When women thrive, societies rise, economies grow, communities strengthen, the future expands. We can give respect, justice, equal pay, safety, education, mentorship, funding, visibility, opportunities, truth, time and voice. We can give by calling out stereotypes, by challenging discrimination, by questioning bias, and by celebrating women's success loudly and unapologetically. Give to gain reminds us of a simple truth: gender equality is not a women's issue, it is a human issue. It belongs in homes, in classrooms, in boardrooms, in courtrooms, in communities, in governments, and in everyday decisions. For over a century, since 1911, International Women's Day has belonged to everyone who believes in equality. As Gloria Steinem once said, "The story of women's struggle for equality belongs to no single feminist nor to any one organization but to the collective efforts of all who care about human rights." This movement is inclusive, global, and unstoppable. This year, we refuse to step back, no matter how deeply rooted the sexism, no matter how discouraging the politics, no matter how loud the resistance. We climb together because 286 years is unacceptable, because 64% is injustice, because silence is complicity. On 8 March 2026 and every day beyond it, we demand rights, not promises; justice, not excuses; action, not delays for all women and girls. And we act by choosing to give to gain, because equality will not wait, and neither will we.

I wasn't afraid of being judged, I was afraid of becoming a burden, so I carried everything myself until my own heart began to feel too heavy to lift. title: Ultrasound-CLIP(CVPR 2026)
transcription: Based on UDT, we propose Ultrasound Clip, a semantic-aware contrastive pre-training framework for ultrasound image-text understanding. First, UDT standardizes ultrasound semantics across different organs and diagnostic scenarios. Then, a UDT-guided heterogeneous graph encoder models relationships among anatomical structures and diagnostic attributes. We further use cross-attention to inject structured semantic knowledge into the text representations. In addition, we construct semantic priors to provide soft semantic supervision during contrastive learning. Together, these modules help align ultrasound images with graph-enhanced and semantically aware text representations. We evaluate Ultrasound Clip on both retrieval and downstream classification tasks. Our method consistently outperforms existing medical vision-language models, including CLIP, PMC-CLIP, and UniMed-CLIP. In retrieval tasks, Ultrasound Clip achieves substantial improvements in both image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval performance. We also observe strong generalization ability across zero-shot, linear probing, and fine-tuning settings. In addition, the qualitative case studies show that our framework captures more accurate diagnostic semantics and produces better image-text alignment. In summary, we present US-365K, the first large-scale dedicated ultrasound image-text dataset, together with Ultrasound Clip, a semantic-aware framework for ultrasound vision-language pre-training. By incorporating structured sonographic knowledge into contrastive learning, our method achieves strong performance and generalization across multiple tasks. Thank you for watching.

title: Why Most People Journal Wrong
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: They fail once, therefore they start questioning their identity. But journaling creates distance. It slows your thoughts down long enough for you to actually observe them. And that changes everything, because when you can observe your thoughts clearly, you stop becoming controlled by every emotion that appears. Imagine sitting down to study, you open the assignment, you stare at the screen for a few seconds, and suddenly your brain wants to do literally anything else. So you check your phone just for a minute, then a minute becomes 20, and eventually the guilt appears again, so you tell yourself, "I need more discipline." But maybe the real problem isn't discipline at all. Maybe you've attached your self-worth so heavily to achievement, that even starting feels emotionally threatening. So instead of risking failure, your brain chooses avoidance, and journaling forces a deeper question: what am I actually feeling right now? Fear? Pressure? Perfectionism? Exhaustion? Because sometimes the problem isn't laziness, sometimes the problem is that your mind is overwhelmed and you've never slowed down enough to notice it. And this is important because awareness changes the quality of your decisions. When you understand what's happening internally, you stop fighting imaginary problems, you stop labeling yourself incorrectly, and slowly your reactions become more intentional. But clarity alone isn't the deepest part of journaling, because eventually, your journal starts revealing patterns. This is where journaling becomes uncomfortable because over time, the same thoughts start appearing again and again. The same fears, the same excuses, the same emotional reactions, and most people never notice these patterns because they spend their entire lives distracting themselves from silence. Carl Jung once said, "Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate." And journaling is one of the simplest ways to make your inner world visible, not to judge yourself, but to understand yourself honestly. I think that's why self-awareness feels uncomfortable for so many people, because eventually, you start realizing how much of your life has been automatic,

title: Gen AI in Libraries Conference Poster on AI Tools for Literature Reviews: A Rubric for Evaluation
transcription: Our poster presentation documents the creation of a rubric by a group of librarians at American University to evaluate which AI tools, if any, made sense for us to subscribe to and promote. We ended up creating this rubric ourselves because we couldn't find an already extant tool that fit our needs, and we thought detailing our process might be helpful to other institutions currently considering the adoption of AI tools. Our university librarian asked our department to pilot an AI research tool. This group then decided to review AI tools focused on the literature review process. Literature review tools were selected for a few reasons. One, they're discipline agnostic. We're a social science heavy institution, which tends to be pretty interdisciplinary. Two, faculty, students, and staff all do literature reviews. And three, there are a number of AI tools with literature reviews built specifically in mind. In order to determine how we would evaluate these tools, we met as a group and discussed what we would want a rubric to measure. We reviewed some of the literature related to this, there wasn't much, and determined the questions by consensus. We then created a survey in Qualtrics. We divided up the list evenly between group members, with some claiming tools in which they were particularly interested or had experience with. Then, each member analyzed three to four tools and recorded the results in Qualtrics. Ithaka, the nonprofit behind JSTOR, has created the Ithaka Generative AI Product Tracker that lists generative AI tools that can be used for postsecondary teaching, learning, or research activities. The tracker includes roughly 150 AI tools and counting, many of which support key stages of the research lifecycle, including discovery, understanding, and creation. We went through the entire list and identified 18 AI tools that could help in the literature review process in subject areas within the curriculum at AU. We then developed a shared evaluation framework based on eight criteria. They include, one, access model, whether the tool is free or subscription-based...

title: The Anxiety Trick No One Talks About (True Student Story)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You don't wait for motivation to act. You act, and motivation follows. Brick by brick, he rebuilt what fear had torn down. If you've ever carried this weight, take a second to like this video, subscribe, and comment, "I am reclaiming my peace." You never know who needs to read it tonight. Three. The tool. Nobody talks about Alex's anxiety didn't vanish because he stopped feeling scared. It changed when he stopped treating thoughts as facts. This is cognitive defusion. Watching a thought pass like a car on a highway instead of climbing in and driving. "I'm going to fail" became "I'm having the thought that I'm going to fail." Small shift in language, massive shift in power. The panic attacks didn't stop overnight, but their grip loosened, and a loosened grip is where freedom quietly begins. Four. Stepping back into the arena. By second semester, Alex signed up to present at a national student conference. The old Alex would have found six reasons to quit, but courage was never the absence of fear. It was walking forward with it anyway. His hands still shook that morning, but he let the feeling exist beside him instead of fighting it. He stood up, he spoke. The anxiety hadn't vanished to let him succeed. He'd succeeded while carrying it the whole time. He went on to earn a research award most students only dream of. But the trophy was never the point. The reflection. Alex's greatness didn't happen in spite of his anxiety. It happened because he learned to walk beside it instead of running from it. A racing heart never fully disappeared, but he built a relationship with his own mind based on understanding instead of war. If you're in your own quiet battle right now, you don't need to defeat every anxious thought today. You just need one brick, one sentence of distance between you and the fear. transcription: Sunny days are overrated. That's what I just kept thinking about in this moment. Chasing sun was only a part of a program they gave us. And maybe that's where we get it wrong. Anxiety is not that bad. But, like all things, complexity seems to creep in. The human mind is quite complex. Deals with many things, calculates many decisions, and makes judgments every moment. It is said that mental pain is less dramatic than physical pain. Both are hard to carry, but mental pain seems to stay a little longer. This message hit harder when I landed in South Africa. I didn't really understand it, but at that point, when I reflect on it now as I edit this video, it really hit me. This was a place I always wondered about, place I imagined, place I only saw in pictures and videos, and then I actually was here. And all I can see is the small things that I've never seen before. Different air, different sky, different road in front of me. And you would think at a moment like this, it would be perfect. But then I felt it, that little tiny itch of anxiety. Not some big panic attack, no heavy breathing, just a feeling inside like something was still trying to get my attention. I started asking myself, why is this even here? I'm in the place I always wanted to see, across the ocean, took the longest plane ride of my life, and I'm standing inside something I used to only imagine. So why am I still feeling a little unsettled, uneasy? And maybe that's what anxiety does. It follows you into beautiful places, not always to ruin them. title: Admiral McRaven: The Letter His Mother Wrote Him Before He Left for SEAL Training
transcription: Outside my B-hut was a wartime environment. Unfortunately, every week we lost kids in combat. Uh, you know, civilians were inadvertently killed. Some Admiral, some General, some President, some Prime Minister, somebody was yelling at me about something outside that door. And my days were long, I mean, my average day was probably 20 hours a day, and some days you'd go days before getting back to that room. But when I got back to the room and I opened my plywood door, the bed was made. And it gave me some sense of control of my life. And and it, I mean, again, hard to kind of square the circle on why that's the case but when when you open the room and the bed is made there's a sense of order. And I've told folks, look, it's a simple task but I really do think it makes a difference. Certainly makes a difference for me. I started to tell you the story but I held off on it earlier today. Um, when I was the chancellor, I was uh, I'd finished up my times as chancellor, I'm getting ready to leave, I'm moving out of the Bower house, which is where the chancellor lives, and we're packing up boxes. And in this box, I find a letter. And it's a letter from my mother, who died back in 1986, but I look at the date on the letter, and it is the date that I went off to SEAL training. It's August 1977. And I realize that she wrote this letter the day that she dropped me off at my aunt's house because she wanted to drive me to SEAL training. I said, "Mother, you're not going to drive me to SEAL training." So, she drove me to my aunt's house in Scottsdale, Arizona. And I was like, I convinced her to stay there and then I continued on. But she had written this letter when she was at Scottsdale. And now, I'm seeing it for the first time. Again, she died in 1986. And of course, I see the letter, it's got her handwriting, and no kidding, and I think my sisters are here in the audience, I could still smell the scent of kind of cold cream and whatever women used back then. And so, I'm I'm opening this letter, and I'm I'm getting kind of emotional. I'm like, oh my god, I opened the letter and it's, my mother would always start the letter, "Dearest Bill," you know. She had...

title: Podcast Interview Excerpt
transcription: I'm Tim Westerbeck, president of Eduvantis, a data-driven strategic marketing firm serving more than 100 of the world's top higher education institutions. Jody Angelo, Dean of the Haub School of Business at Saint Joseph's University in Philadelphia, joins the Business Education Revolution podcast. We'll discuss the flood of mergers and acquisitions reshaping today's higher education competitive environment. Joe is a veteran of the M&A landscape in higher education going back decades. He's also on the front line of today's new M&A reality, having within the last year been deeply involved in several major acquisitions at his institution. How much of what's going on in this market that we're talking about, in your opinion, is truly strategic? Strategic meaning, if we're going to acquire this party, it's because we have a very clear purpose in mind, uh, to do something that will enhance our enterprise. It isn't just, well, there's some discounted real estate here and some more students. And vice versa, um, if I'm, uh, having financial difficulties and I'm looking for a party to acquire me, is it just to save my financial bacon or is it, uh, uh, how much is strategic, in your view? Well, that's, that's where you need to really, uh, be on your game because we've had four or five schools come to us over the last several years wanting to merge, where we said no, um, because, one, their programs didn't complement, uh, the other, their financial situation was, um, too, too dire. Um, or we didn't quite need what they had, uh, you know, for our, for our programs. So, you know, you've got to, you've got to do your homework. It's just not like every, every two institutions can say, hey, let's just put our programs together. 25 years ago, yeah, you were looking for other campuses, uh, because that's what you needed to do to offer classes.
